1.title: Responsible AI
1.text: Welcome to Module eleven: Responsible A I. This module opens Domain four, and covers task statement four point one. You will learn the features of responsible A I, the data and the tools that support it, how Amazon Bedrock Guardrails works, how to choose models responsibly, and the legal risks of generative A I. The exam gives you a symptom or a need and asks you to name the feature, the tool or the risk.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Identify the features of responsible A I: bias, fairness, inclusivity, robustness, safety and veracity. Use tools such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Select models responsibly, with sustainability in mind. Name the legal risks of generative A I. And describe datasets, bias and variance, and the tools that detect and monitor bias.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedar and Salt Faces Questions of Trust
1.text: At Cedar and Salt Travel, a reviewer notices that the assistant serves English speakers better. It once invented a refund rule, and a guest's email address appeared in a chat. Leaders ask which model is responsible to run, and what the legal risks are. Your job is to choose the checks, tools and data that build trust.

1.title: Features of Responsible AI
1.text: The picture shows A W S's eight core dimensions of responsible A I: fairness, explainability, privacy and security, safety, controllability, veracity and robustness, governance and transparency. The exam guide names six features. Bias is systematic unfairness in data or outputs. Fairness considers the impact on different groups. Inclusivity means the system works for people of all backgrounds. Robustness means correct outputs, even with unexpected or adversarial inputs. Safety means preventing harmful output and misuse. And veracity means truthful, correct outputs. Exam tip: match the symptom to the feature. Unequal results is fairness, harmful output is safety, and invented facts is veracity.

1.title: Bias and Its Effects
1.text: Bias can enter through unrepresentative data, inconsistent labels, the model itself, or the prompt. The effects are worse results for some demographic groups, inaccurate answers, unfair decisions and lost trust. At Cedar and Salt, summaries of reviews written in less common languages come out poorer. You reduce bias with balanced, diverse data, tests by group, Guardrails and human audits. No single fix removes bias, so keep monitoring. Exam tip: unequal results across groups point to bias and fairness, so check the data first.

1.title: Characteristics of Responsible Datasets
1.text: What does a responsible dataset look like? Inclusivity: it covers all the groups, languages and regions the system serves. Diversity: many viewpoints, styles and situations. Curated sources: trusted, documented and licensed sources, checked before use. Balanced: no group or class dominates the data. And label quality: labels are correct and consistent between reviewers. Exam tip: inclusive, diverse, curated and balanced are the four words to remember for data.

1.title: Bias and Variance
1.text: Bias and variance describe two ways a model can go wrong. Underfitting is high bias: the model misses the pattern and is inaccurate for everyone. Overfitting is high variance: the model memorizes its training data, and fails on new data and on groups that were not in it. A good fit is balanced, and works on training and new data. Biased data can also make a model systematically worse for a demographic group. Fix underfitting with a richer model or better features, and overfitting with more varied data and simpler models. Exam tip: great on training data and poor on new data is overfitting, which is high variance.

1.title: Detecting and Monitoring Bias, Trust and Truthfulness
1.text: How do you detect and monitor problems? To analyze label quality, check labels for errors and disagreement, by reviewing samples with your experts. For human audits, people inspect samples of outputs; Amazon A two I supports human review of predictions, and Bedrock offers human evaluation. For subgroup analysis, compare results across groups; Amazon SageMaker Clarify detects bias before and after training, and over time. For truthfulness, and for toxicity and robustness, use Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation. Exam tip: bias in data and predictions means SageMaker Clarify, and people reviewing outputs means Amazon A two I.

1.title: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: The Safeguards
1.text: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails offers six safeguards. Content filters detect hate, insults, sexual content, violence, misconduct and prompt attacks, with adjustable strength. Denied topics block subjects you define as off-limits. Word filters block custom words or phrases, such as profanity or competitor names. Sensitive information filters block or mask personally identifiable information, and custom patterns. Contextual grounding checks detect hallucinations that are not grounded in the source. And Automated Reasoning checks validate answers against logical rules. Exam tip: to mask personal data, use the sensitive information filter; for an ungrounded R A G answer, use the contextual grounding check.

1.title: How Guardrails Works
1.text: The picture shows a guardrail around a model call. The input is checked first. If it violates a policy, your blocked message is returned and the model call is discarded. If it passes, the model answers, and then the response is checked; it is blocked or masked if it violates a policy. You can use a guardrail with model calls, or on its own through the Apply Guardrail A P I. It works with Agents and Knowledge Bases, but embedding and image models are not supported. You pay for the policies you configure. Exam tip: one guardrail can protect many models, and it checks both what goes in and what comes out.

1.title: Responsible Model Selection and Sustainability
1.text: Responsible model selection includes sustainability. First, ask whether generative A I is the right tool; a simpler approach may use far less energy. Right-size the model: a smaller model that meets the quality bar uses fewer resources. Customize efficiently: fine-tune a small model for the task, or distill a large one. Scale with demand: auto scaling and serverless services avoid idle capacity. And check the evaluation evidence for bias, toxicity and robustness before you choose. Exam tip: the responsible choice is the smallest model that does the job, run only when needed.

2.title: Legal Risks of Generative AI
2.text: This slide goes beyond the guide, and it is general guidance, not legal advice. There are five legal risks. Intellectual property claims: output may resemble protected work, or data rights may be questioned; read the provider terms, document your data sources, and review outputs. Biased outputs can bring discrimination complaints; use balanced data, subgroup tests and Guardrails. Loss of customer trust damages the brand; disclose A I use, add filters and open feedback channels. End user risk, such as harmful advice or exposed personal data; use Guardrails, and human review for high stakes. And hallucinations mislead users; ground answers with R A G. Involve legal counsel.

2.title: Veracity and Robustness
2.text: For veracity, reduce hallucinations with R A G grounding, contextual grounding checks and review. For robustness, test with rephrased, misspelled and unusual input; Amazon Bedrock scores semantic robustness. Defend against adversarial input with the prompt attack filter, and the layered defenses from Module eight. Keep people in the loop for decisions with high impact. And monitor in production, because behavior drifts. Exam tip: invented facts is veracity, fixed by grounding, and fragile to odd input is robustness.

2.title: Responsible AI in Practice
2.text: Here is responsible A I in practice. Define who could be harmed, and how. Use balanced, curated data, and choose a right-sized model with evaluation evidence. Add Guardrails for harmful content, personal data and ungrounded answers. Test by subgroup, and run human audits. Review the workload with the A W S Well-Architected Tool and the Generative A I Lens. Monitor bias and feedback after launch, and keep humans in the loop for high-impact decisions. And document the model and the data, which is the topic of Module twelve. Exam tip: responsible A I is a loop of design, test, guard, monitor and document.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Responsible AI
2.text: Here is how the exam frames this module. Which feature: bias, fairness, inclusivity, robustness, safety or veracity. Which tool: Guardrails for filtering, SageMaker Clarify for bias, and Amazon A two I for human review. Which data trait: inclusive, diverse, curated or balanced. Which problem: high bias is underfitting, and high variance is overfitting. And which legal risk: I P claims, biased output, lost trust, end user risk or hallucinations. Exam tip: name the symptom first, then the feature, tool or risk.

2.title: Design Check: Cedar and Salt's Trust Review
2.text: Now a design check. Cover the right column and name the answer. The assistant serves English speakers better: bias, so add multilingual data and test by group. Ninety percent of reviews come from one region: an unbalanced dataset, so collect diverse, balanced data. Staff want competitor talk blocked: denied topics or word filters. Guest emails appear in chat: the sensitive information filter. The assistant invents a refund rule: a contextual grounding check and R A G. A high score on training reviews but poor on new ones: overfitting. And cutting energy use for chat: a right-sized, smaller model. Pause the video if you want more time.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. The features are bias, fairness, inclusivity, robustness, safety and veracity. Good data is inclusive, diverse, curated and balanced, with label quality checked. Underfitting is high bias, and overfitting is high variance. The tools are Guardrails, SageMaker Clarify, Amazon A two I and Bedrock Model Evaluation. And selection and law: choose right-sized, efficient models, and know the I P, bias, trust, end user and hallucination risks.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Which Amazon Bedrock Guardrails safeguard can block or mask personally identifiable information in prompts and responses? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: sensitive information filters. They block or mask P I I, and can use custom patterns. Content filters detect harmful categories, denied topics block subjects, and word filters block custom words.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Cedar and Salt's R A G assistant sometimes states policies that are not in the retrieved documents. Which Guardrails safeguard helps detect this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: contextual grounding checks. They detect hallucinations when a response is not grounded in the source, which fits R A G applications. The other safeguards do not compare an answer with its sources.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Select two. Which two are legal risks of working with generative A I? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Legal risks include intellectual property infringement claims, biased outputs, loss of customer trust, end user risk and hallucinations. Speed, context size and price are not legal risks.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A model scores well on its training data but poorly on new data, especially for groups missing from the training set. What does this indicate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: overfitting, which is high variance. The model memorizes its training data and fails on new data. More varied, representative data helps, and subgroup analysis reveals the gap.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Which dataset best supports building a fair model? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: a curated set that is balanced and inclusive. Responsible datasets are inclusive, diverse, curated and balanced, with good label quality. One source, one group, or unchecked labels build in bias.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Which choice best supports responsible, sustainable model selection for a simple summarization task? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: choose a right-sized model that meets the quality need. The Well-Architected Generative A I Lens recommends right-sized models, efficient customization, and capacity that scales with demand.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all six answers. Question one: C. Question two: A. Question three: B and D. Question four: B. Question five: D. Question six: C. That completes Module eleven. Next, Module twelve looks at transparent and explainable models, and how to document them.
